title: States of Matter
description: Class 11 Chemistry States of Matter: gas laws, ideal gas equation PV=nRT, kinetic theory, molecular speeds, real gases, van der Waals equation and liquids.

topics.title: Gas Laws & Ideal Gas Equation
topics.concept:
Matter exists in three familiar physical states — solid, liquid and gas — and the same substance can move between them by changing temperature or pressure. What decides the state is the tug-of-war between the intermolecular forces that pull molecules together and the thermal energy that keeps them moving apart.

Intermolecular forces (van der Waals forces) are much weaker than chemical bonds. Three types matter here:

  • London dispersion forces — momentary dipoles in every atom or molecule; they grow with molecular size and explain why larger non-polar molecules have higher boiling points.
  • Dipole–dipole forces — act between permanent dipoles in polar molecules such as $\text{HCl}$.
  • Hydrogen bonding — a specially strong dipole attraction when H is bonded to the small, highly electronegative atoms N, O or F (as in water and ammonia).

Gases have the weakest grip of these forces relative to their thermal energy, so they fill any container. Their behaviour is summarised by simple gas laws, each relating two variables while the others stay fixed.

Boyle’s law (constant $T$, fixed $n$): pressure is inversely proportional to volume, $P\propto\frac{1}{V}$, so $P_1V_1=P_2V_2$.

Charles’ law (constant $P$): volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature, $\frac{V}{T}=\text{constant}$, so $\frac{V_1}{T_1}=\frac{V_2}{T_2}$.

Gay-Lussac’s law (constant $V$): pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature, $\frac{P}{T}=\text{constant}$.

Avogadro’s law: at the same $T$ and $P$, equal volumes contain equal numbers of molecules, so $V\propto n$. One mole of any gas occupies $22.4\ \text{L}$ at STP.

Combining all four gives the combined gas law $\frac{P_1V_1}{T_1}=\frac{P_2V_2}{T_2}$ and the ideal gas equation $PV=nRT$, where $R=8.314\ \text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}=0.0821\ \text{L}\,\text{atm}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$.

For a mixture of non-reacting gases, Dalton’s law of partial pressures states $P_{total}=p_1+p_2+\dots$, and each partial pressure equals the total pressure times that gas’s mole fraction: $p_i=x_i\,P_{total}$. A key reminder: every temperature in these laws must be in kelvin, $T(\text{K})=t(^\circ\text{C})+273.15$.

examples.problem: A gas occupies 2.0 L at 760 mmHg. What volume will it occupy at 380 mmHg, temperature constant?
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Boyle’s law (constant $T$): $P_1V_1=P_2V_2$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $760\times2.0=380\times V_2$.
  3. Step 3: Solve: $V_2=\frac{1520}{380}=4.0\ \text{L}$.

Answer: $V_2=4.0\ \text{L}$ (halving the pressure doubles the volume).

examples.problem: A gas has a volume of 300 mL at $27^\circ\text{C}$. Find its volume at $127^\circ\text{C}$ at constant pressure.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Convert to kelvin: $T_1=300\ \text{K}$, $T_2=400\ \text{K}$.
  2. Step 2: Charles’ law: $\frac{V_1}{T_1}=\frac{V_2}{T_2}$.
  3. Step 3: $V_2=300\times\frac{400}{300}=400\ \text{mL}$.

Answer: $V_2=400\ \text{mL}$.

examples.problem: The pressure of a fixed-volume gas is 1.5 atm at $27^\circ\text{C}$. Find the pressure at $327^\circ\text{C}$.
How many moles of an ideal gas occupy 4.92 L at 2.0 atm and 300 K? ($R=0.0821\ \text{L atm mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$)
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Ideal gas equation: $PV=nRT\Rightarrow n=\frac{PV}{RT}$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $n=\frac{2.0\times4.92}{0.0821\times300}$.
  3. Step 3: $n=\frac{9.84}{24.63}\approx0.40\ \text{mol}$.

Answer: $n\approx0.40\ \text{mol}$.

examples.problem: A 2.0 L flask at 300 K contains 0.20 mol $\text{N}_2$ and 0.30 mol $\text{O}_2$. Find the partial pressure of $\text{O}_2$. ($R=0.0821$)
A gas at 1 atm and 273 K has a density of $1.25\ \text{g/L}$. Find its molar mass. ($R=0.0821$)
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: From $PV=nRT$ and $n=\frac{m}{M}$, density form is $M=\frac{dRT}{P}$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $M=\frac{1.25\times0.0821\times273}{1}$.
  3. Step 3: $M\approx28.0\ \text{g/mol}$ (i.e. $\text{N}_2$).

Answer: $M\approx28\ \text{g/mol}$.

recap: Intermolecular forces (London dispersion, dipole–dipole, hydrogen bonding) compete with thermal energy to decide the physical state; gases have the weakest relative grip.
Boyle’s law: $P\propto\frac{1}{V}$ at constant $T$; Charles’ law: $\frac{V}{T}=\text{constant}$ at constant $P$; Gay-Lussac’s law: $\frac{P}{T}=\text{constant}$ at constant $V$.
Avogadro’s law: $V\propto n$ at fixed $T,P$; one mole of any gas occupies $22.4\ \text{L}$ at STP.
Dalton’s law: $P_{total}=p_1+p_2+\dots$ and $p_i=x_i\,P_{total}$; always use absolute temperature in kelvin.

quiz.q: At constant temperature, if the volume of a fixed mass of gas is reduced to one-third, its pressure becomes:
quiz.explanation: Boyle’s law: $P\propto\frac{1}{V}$, so reducing $V$ to $\frac{1}{3}$ triples $P$.

quiz.q: Which temperature scale must be used in the gas laws?
quiz.explanation: Gas-law proportionalities hold only for absolute (kelvin) temperature, where $0\ \text{K}$ is true zero.

quiz.q: Equal volumes of two gases at the same $T$ and $P$ contain equal numbers of molecules. This is:
quiz.explanation: Avogadro’s law links volume directly to the number of molecules (moles).

quiz.q: In a gas mixture, the partial pressure of a component equals:
options: total pressure divided by number of gases
total pressure times number of moles
quiz.explanation: By Dalton’s law, $p_i=x_i P_{total}$, where $x_i$ is the mole fraction.

topics.title: Kinetic Theory & Molecular Speeds
topics.concept:
The gas laws are experimental facts. The kinetic molecular theory of gases explains why they hold by modelling a gas as a vast crowd of tiny molecules in ceaseless, random motion. The model rests on a few postulates:

  • A gas consists of a large number of identical molecules whose total volume is negligible compared with the container.
  • Molecules are in constant random motion, travelling in straight lines until they collide.
  • There are no attractive or repulsive forces between molecules except during collisions.
  • Collisions (with each other and the walls) are perfectly elastic — no kinetic energy is lost.
  • The average kinetic energy of the molecules is directly proportional to the absolute temperature.

Working out the force of wall collisions gives the kinetic-theory pressure relation $PV=\frac{1}{3}mN\,\overline{u^2}$, where $m$ is the molecular mass, $N$ the number of molecules and $\overline{u^2}$ the mean-square speed. Comparing with $PV=nRT$ shows that the average translational kinetic energy per molecule is $\overline{KE}=\frac{3}{2}k_BT$, where $k_B=\frac{R}{N_A}=1.38\times10^{-23}\ \text{J/K}$. So temperature is a direct measure of molecular kinetic energy — raise $T$ and the molecules move faster.

Because molecules collide constantly, they do not all share one speed; instead there is a spread. Three average speeds are useful:

  • Most probable speed $u_{mp}=\sqrt{\frac{2RT}{M}}$ — the peak of the distribution, the speed possessed by the largest fraction of molecules.
  • Average speed $u_{avg}=\sqrt{\frac{8RT}{\pi M}}$ — the simple arithmetic mean.
  • Root-mean-square speed $u_{rms}=\sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}$ — the square root of the mean-square speed; it links directly to kinetic energy.

Their fixed ratio is $u_{mp}:u_{avg}:u_{rms}=1:1.128:1.224$, so $u_{mp}

The full spread of speeds is described by the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution. Its curve rises from zero, peaks at $u_{mp}$, then tails off at high speed. As temperature rises the peak shifts to higher speed and broadens and flattens — the molecules speed up and the spread widens — while the total area (total number of molecules) stays constant. Lighter gases (smaller $M$) move faster at the same temperature, which is why hydrogen escapes a balloon faster than nitrogen.

examples.problem: Calculate the rms speed of $\text{N}_2$ molecules ($M=0.028\ \text{kg/mol}$) at 300 K. ($R=8.314$)
Find the most probable speed of $\text{O}_2$ ($M=0.032\ \text{kg/mol}$) at 300 K.
For a gas the rms speed is $500\ \text{m/s}$. Find its average speed.
By what factor does the rms speed change when the temperature of a gas is raised from 300 K to 1200 K?
Find the average translational kinetic energy of one gas molecule at 300 K. ($k_B=1.38\times10^{-23}\ \text{J/K}$)
At the same temperature, compare the rms speeds of $\text{He}$ ($M=4$) and $\text{O}_2$ ($M=32$).
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: At fixed $T$, $u_{rms}\propto\frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}$, so $\frac{u_{He}}{u_{O_2}}=\sqrt{\frac{M_{O_2}}{M_{He}}}$.
  2. Step 2: $\frac{u_{He}}{u_{O_2}}=\sqrt{\frac{32}{4}}=\sqrt{8}$.
  3. Step 3: $\frac{u_{He}}{u_{O_2}}\approx2.83$.

Answer: Helium moves about $2.83$ times faster than oxygen.

recap: Kinetic theory models a gas as many tiny molecules in constant random motion, with negligible volume, no inter-molecular forces except at collisions, and perfectly elastic collisions.
Kinetic pressure relation: $PV=\frac{1}{3}mN\,\overline{u^2}$; average translational KE per molecule $=\frac{3}{2}k_BT$, so temperature measures molecular kinetic energy.
The Maxwell–Boltzmann curve peaks at $u_{mp}$; raising $T$ shifts the peak right and flattens the curve, while lighter gases move faster at the same temperature.

quiz.q: According to kinetic theory, the average kinetic energy of gas molecules depends only on:
quiz.explanation: $\overline{KE}=\frac{3}{2}k_BT$ depends only on $T$, not on the gas’s identity.

quiz.q: The correct order of molecular speeds is:
If the absolute temperature of a gas is quadrupled, its rms speed becomes:
quiz.explanation: $u_{rms}\propto\sqrt{T}$, so a 4× increase in $T$ doubles the speed.

quiz.q: On the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve, raising temperature causes the peak to:
options: shift to lower speed and sharpen
shift to higher speed and flatten
quiz.explanation: Higher $T$ moves the most-probable speed up and broadens (flattens) the distribution.

topics.title: Real Gases & Liquid State
topics.concept:
The ideal gas equation works beautifully at low pressure and high temperature, but every real gas deviates from it under other conditions. The reason is that two ideal assumptions break down: real molecules do occupy finite volume, and they do exert attractive forces on one another.

The cleanest way to measure deviation is the compressibility factor $Z=\frac{PV}{nRT}$. For an ideal gas $Z=1$ at all conditions. For a real gas:

  • At low pressure, attractive forces dominate, pulling molecules together and reducing volume, so $Z<1$.
  • At high pressure, the finite molecular volume dominates and the gas is harder to compress, so $Z>1$.
  • $\text{H}_2$ and $\text{He}$ (very weak attractions) show $Z>1$ at almost all pressures.

To repair the ideal equation, van der Waals introduced two corrections. The measured pressure is less than ideal because attractions slow molecules approaching the wall, so we add $\frac{an^2}{V^2}$; the free space is less than the container volume because molecules themselves take up room, so we subtract $nb$. This gives the van der Waals equation: $\left(P+\frac{an^2}{V^2}\right)(V-nb)=nRT$, where $a$ measures the strength of attraction and $b$ the effective molecular volume.

When a gas is cooled and compressed enough, attractions win and it liquefies. But there is a limit: above the critical temperature $T_c$, no amount of pressure can liquefy a gas. The pressure needed to liquefy it exactly at $T_c$ is the critical pressure $P_c$, and the volume of one mole then is the critical volume $V_c$. These critical constants relate to the van der Waals constants: $T_c=\frac{8a}{27Rb}$, $P_c=\frac{a}{27b^2}$, $V_c=3b$.

Once liquefied, the substance shows the distinctive properties of liquids:

  • Vapour pressure — the pressure of vapour in equilibrium with its liquid; it rises with temperature, and a liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure.
  • Surface tension ($\gamma$) — the inward pull on surface molecules that minimises surface area, causing droplets to be spherical and water to rise in a capillary; it decreases as temperature rises.
  • Viscosity ($\eta$) — a liquid’s resistance to flow, arising from internal friction between layers; it too decreases with rising temperature as molecules gain energy to slide past one another.

examples.problem: At 300 K and 5 atm, 2.0 mol of a gas occupies 9.0 L. Find its compressibility factor $Z$. ($R=0.0821$)
For a real gas $Z=1.05$ at high pressure. What does this indicate about the dominant effect?
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: $Z=\frac{PV}{nRT}>1$ means the actual volume exceeds the ideal prediction.
  2. Step 2: This excess volume comes from the molecules’ own finite size (the $b$ term).
  3. Step 3: Hence repulsion / finite molecular volume dominates at high pressure.

Answer: Finite molecular volume (repulsive effect) dominates, making the gas less compressible than ideal.

examples.problem: For $\text{CO}_2$, $a=3.6\ \text{L}^2\text{atm mol}^{-2}$ and $b=0.043\ \text{L/mol}$. Estimate the critical temperature. ($R=0.0821$)
The van der Waals constant $b$ for a gas is $0.0428\ \text{L/mol}$. Find its critical volume per mole.
A liquid in an open dish boils when its vapour pressure reaches 1 atm at $78^\circ\text{C}$. What happens to its boiling point on a high mountain where external pressure is 0.7 atm?
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: A liquid boils when vapour pressure equals external pressure.
  2. Step 2: Lower external pressure (0.7 atm) is reached at a lower vapour pressure, hence a lower temperature.
  3. Step 3: Therefore the boiling point falls below $78^\circ\text{C}$.

Answer: The boiling point decreases at lower external pressure.

examples.problem: Among $\text{He}$, $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{NH}_3$, which is the easiest to liquefy and why?
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Ease of liquefaction tracks the strength of intermolecular attraction (larger van der Waals $a$, higher $T_c$).
  2. Step 2: $\text{NH}_3$ has hydrogen bonding (strongest attraction); $\text{N}_2$ has only weak dispersion; $\text{He}$ has the weakest of all.
  3. Step 3: So $\text{NH}_3$ has the highest critical temperature.

Answer: $\text{NH}_3$ is easiest to liquefy because hydrogen bonding gives it the strongest attractions and highest $T_c$.

recap: Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour because molecules have finite volume and exert attractive forces; deviation is largest at high pressure and low temperature.
Compressibility factor $Z=\frac{PV}{nRT}$: $Z=1$ for an ideal gas; $Z<1$ when attractions dominate (low $P$) and $Z>1$ when molecular volume dominates (high $P$).
van der Waals equation: $\left(P+\frac{an^2}{V^2}\right)(V-nb)=nRT$, where $a$ measures attraction and $b$ the molecular volume.
A gas cannot be liquefied above its critical temperature $T_c$; critical constants relate to van der Waals constants by $T_c=\frac{8a}{27Rb}$, $P_c=\frac{a}{27b^2}$, $V_c=3b$.
Liquid properties: vapour pressure rises with temperature (boiling when it equals external pressure); surface tension and viscosity both decrease as temperature rises.

quiz.q: For an ideal gas the compressibility factor $Z$ is:
quiz.explanation: By definition $Z=\frac{PV}{nRT}=1$ for an ideal gas under all conditions.

quiz.q: In the van der Waals equation, the term $\frac{an^2}{V^2}$ corrects for:
quiz.explanation: The pressure-correction term accounts for attractive forces that lower the measured pressure.

quiz.q: A gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone if it is above its:
quiz.explanation: Above $T_c$ molecular kinetic energy always exceeds the attractions, so no pressure can liquefy the gas.

quiz.q: As temperature increases, the surface tension of a liquid:
quiz.explanation: Higher thermal energy weakens the net inward pull on surface molecules, lowering surface tension.

questions.q: Boyle’s law is valid at constant:
questions.explanation: Boyle’s law relates $P$ and $V$ at constant temperature: $PV=\text{constant}$.

questions.q: The ideal gas equation is:
questions.explanation: The ideal gas equation combines all four gas laws into $PV=nRT$.

questions.q: According to Charles’ law, at constant pressure volume is proportional to:
questions.explanation: $\frac{V}{T}=\text{constant}$, so $V\propto T$ (in kelvin).

questions.q: Equal volumes of gases at the same $T$ and $P$ contain equal numbers of molecules. This is:
questions.explanation: Avogadro’s law: $V\propto n$ at fixed $T,P$.

questions.q: Hydrogen bonding is strongest when H is bonded to:
questions.explanation: Among the listed atoms only F (highly electronegative and small) gives true hydrogen bonding.

questions.q: The value of $R$ in $\text{L atm mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ is:
In Dalton’s law, the partial pressure of a gas equals:
questions.explanation: $p_i=x_i P_{total}$, with $x_i$ the mole fraction.

questions.q: The average translational kinetic energy of a molecule is:
questions.explanation: Kinetic theory gives $\overline{KE}=\frac{3}{2}k_BT$ per molecule.

questions.q: The rms speed of a gas is:
questions.explanation: By definition $u_{rms}=\sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}$.

questions.q: The correct order of molecular speeds is:
questions.explanation: The fixed ratio $1:1.128:1.224$ gives $u_{mp}<u_{avg}<u_{rms}$.

questions.q: If the temperature of a gas is increased four times, the rms speed becomes:
questions.explanation: $u_{rms}\propto\sqrt{T}$, so $\sqrt{4}=2$: the speed doubles.

questions.q: On the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve, raising temperature makes the peak:
questions.explanation: Higher $T$ shifts the most-probable speed to a higher value and broadens (flattens) the curve.

questions.q: The compressibility factor for an ideal gas equals:
questions.explanation: $Z=\frac{PV}{nRT}=1$ for an ideal gas.

questions.q: When attractive forces dominate, the compressibility factor is:
questions.explanation: Attractions reduce the actual volume below ideal, so $Z<1$ (typically at low pressure).

questions.q: In the van der Waals equation, $b$ corrects for:
questions.explanation: The $nb$ term subtracts the volume occupied by molecules themselves.

questions.q: A gas cannot be liquefied by pressure above its:
questions.explanation: Above $T_c$, no pressure can produce a liquid.

questions.q: The critical volume $V_c$ in terms of the van der Waals constant $b$ is:
questions.explanation: Solving the van der Waals critical conditions gives $V_c=3b$.

questions.q: As temperature rises, the viscosity of a liquid:
questions.explanation: Higher temperature gives molecules more energy to slide past each other, lowering viscosity.

questions.q: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure becomes equal to:
questions.explanation: Boiling occurs when vapour pressure equals the surrounding (external) pressure.

questions.q: At the same temperature, which gas has the highest rms speed?
questions.explanation: At fixed $T$, $u_{rms}\propto\frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}$; hydrogen has the smallest molar mass.

questions.q: At constant temperature, a gas at 6 atm occupies 2 L. If compressed to 0.5 L, the pressure is:
questions.explanation: $P_2=\frac{P_1V_1}{V_2}=\frac{6\times2}{0.5}=24\ \text{atm}$.

questions.q: A gas at 300 K is heated until its volume doubles at constant pressure. The new temperature is:
questions.explanation: Charles’ law: $V\propto T$, so doubling $V$ doubles $T$ to $600\ \text{K}$.

questions.q: Two flasks of equal volume at the same $T$ hold $\text{H}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ at equal pressure. The ratio of numbers of molecules $\text{H}_2:\text{O}_2$ is:
questions.explanation: By Avogadro’s law equal $V,T,P$ means equal numbers of molecules, so $1:1$.

questions.q: The ratio $u_{rms}$ of $\text{H}_2$ to $\text{O}_2$ at the same temperature is:
If the rms speed of a gas at 27°C is $v$, its rms speed at 927°C is:
For a real gas at very high pressure, $Z=\frac{PV}{nRT}$ is generally:
questions.explanation: Finite molecular volume dominates at high pressure, giving $Z>1$.

questions.q: For 2 mol of a gas at 500 K and 8.21 atm occupying 10 L, $Z$ is approximately ($R=0.0821$):
A gas has van der Waals constants $a=4.0$, $b=0.05\ \text{L/mol}$. Its critical volume per mole is:
questions.explanation: $V_c=3b=3\times0.05=0.15\ \text{L/mol}$.

questions.q: Which gas is the easiest to liquefy?
questions.explanation: $\text{NH}_3$ has hydrogen bonding, hence the strongest attractions and the highest $T_c$.

questions.q: A mixture has equal masses of $\text{He}$ ($M=4$) and $\text{CH}_4$ ($M=16$). The mole ratio $\text{He}:\text{CH}_4$ is:
questions.explanation: For equal mass $m$, moles $=\frac{m}{M}$, so ratio $=\frac{1/4}{1/16}=4:1$.

questions.q: A 1 L vessel holds $\text{N}_2$ at 0.6 atm and $\text{O}_2$ at 0.4 atm. The mole fraction of $\text{N}_2$ is:
questions.explanation: Total $=1.0$ atm; $x_{\text{N}_2}=\frac{p_{\text{N}_2}}{P_{total}}=\frac{0.6}{1.0}=0.6$.

questions.q: For the Maxwell distribution, raising the temperature keeps which quantity constant?
options: the total area under the curve
questions.explanation: The area equals the total number of molecules, which is conserved; only the shape shifts.

questions.q: A gas obeys $PV=nRT$ best under conditions of:
questions.explanation: At low pressure and high temperature, molecular volume and attractions are negligible, so $Z\to1$.

questions.q: If the average KE of gas molecules is doubled, the absolute temperature is:
questions.explanation: $\overline{KE}=\frac{3}{2}k_BT\propto T$, so doubling KE doubles $T$.
